title: Chapter 6.  Polity & Governance — The LG, the LAHDCs & Current Structure

blocks.content: Ladakh's governance structure is distinctive for combining direct central administration (via the LG) with a relatively empowered pre-existing local self-government system (the LAHDCs) — a hybrid arrangement that pre-dates, and now operates alongside, the region's UT status.

As a UT without a Legislative Assembly, Ladakh is administered directly by a Lieutenant Governor (LG) appointed by the President of India, who exercises both the ceremonial-head and practical executive functions of the territory's administration, advised by a UT Secretariat and Chief Secretary-led bureaucracy, without an elected Chief Minister or Council of Ministers.

Ladakh's LG post has seen relatively rapid turnover compared to some other UTs, with four different Lieutenant Governors holding office in the roughly six-and-a-half years since the UT's creation in October 2019.

cells: First Lieutenant Governor of the new UT
Second LG; tenure included the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council (Kargil) elections and continued Sixth Schedule/statehood agitation
Third LG; tenure spanned the peak of the 2025 unrest (September 2025 Leh violence, Sonam Wangchuk's NSA detention); resigned to become Governor of Himachal Pradesh
Previously Lieutenant Governor of Delhi (2022-2026); transferred to Ladakh as part of a wider gubernatorial/LG reshuffle

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Current (2026) LG of Ladakh: Vinai Kumar Saxena, sworn in 13 March 2026, having previously served as LG of Delhi — a notable case of an LG being transferred directly between two different UTs, a frequently tested current-affairs fact.
The Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDCs)

The LAHDCs for Leh and Kargil are elected local self-government bodies, each headed by a Chief Executive Councillor (CEC), exercising devolved powers over a wide range of subjects including land use, agriculture, health, education, and local taxation — a significantly more empowered local-government model than the standard Panchayati Raj structure found in most of India, reflecting Ladakh's historically distinct governance evolution (Chapter 4).

Following the 2019 UT reorganisation, questions arose regarding the LAHDCs' exact relationship with the new, directly-administered UT structure — since the councils were originally designed to operate as an autonomy layer WITHIN a state government framework, their role and effective powers within a no-Assembly UT (where the LG already holds direct administrative authority) have been a subject of ongoing debate, forming part of the broader statehood/Sixth Schedule discussion in Chapter 7.

LAHDC elections are periodically held (Leh and Kargil on separate election cycles); these have, in recent years, taken on outsized political significance as one of the only direct electoral opportunities available to Ladakhi voters in the absence of a UT-level Legislative Assembly.

cells: Kargil — covers Kargil district, predominantly Shia Muslim-majority

items: The Leh Apex Body (LAB) is an umbrella coalition of political, religious, social and student organisations from the Leh district, formed to collectively advocate for statehood and Sixth Schedule protection.

The Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) is the equivalent umbrella coalition for Kargil district — notably uniting with the LAB (despite Leh's Buddhist-majority and Kargil's Muslim-majority character) in a joint, cross-regional advocacy platform, a significant instance of Ladakh's two districts collaborating on shared political demands despite their differing religious/demographic profiles.
Both bodies have led sustained negotiations with the Union Home Ministry's High-Powered Committee (HPC, formed in 2023) on the statehood and Sixth Schedule demands, detailed fully in Chapter 7.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: LAB (Leh Apex Body) and KDA (Kargil Democratic Alliance) jointly advocating for the SAME demands (statehood + Sixth Schedule) despite representing districts of different religious majorities (Buddhist-majority Leh vs Muslim-majority Kargil) is a frequently highlighted, exam-relevant example of cross-community political unity in the region.

items: Current (2026) LG: Vinai Kumar Saxena, since 13 March 2026 (previously LG of Delhi); LG sequence: R.K. Mathur -> B.D. Mishra -> Kavinder Gupta -> Vinai Kumar Saxena.
LAHDC Leh (est. 1995) and LAHDC Kargil (est. 2003) are elected local self-government bodies, each headed by a Chief Executive Councillor (CEC).
LAB (Leh Apex Body) and KDA (Kargil Democratic Alliance) are the two umbrella civil-society coalitions jointly leading the statehood/Sixth Schedule movement.
High-Powered Committee (HPC), formed by the Union Home Ministry in 2023, is the primary negotiating forum on Ladakh's demands.
